title: Sands of the Ganges (section 11)
hookLine: as many rivers as the Ganges' sands, and worlds of treasure for each: still less than this teaching

lines: A NUMBER TOO BIG FOR NUMBERS.
cards: Scoop a handful of sand from a riverbank and try counting the grains. The count slips long before the hand is empty. Now the Diamond Sutra asks for something stranger.
Take the river Ganges and its sand. For every single grain, add another whole Ganges. Now count the sand in all of those rivers.
The mind gives up somewhere around the second step, and that's the point. When this sutra wants a number too big for numbers, it reaches for river sand.

teach.b: First, the rivers. If there were as many rivers Ganges as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the Buddha asks, would the sand in all of them be much? Very much, Subhuti says; the rivers alone would be beyond counting.
Suppose a good man or a good woman filled as many worlds as there are grains in all those rivers with precious things, and gave it all away. Would the merit be great? Very great, Subhuti says.
Notice the words, a good man or a good woman: both are named, here and elsewhere in this sutra. Third, the turn.
Yet if a good man or a good woman keeps even four lines of this sutra and explains them to others, the Buddha says, that merit is greater. Fourth, why say it twice?
Section eight already set four lines against a world system of treasure. Here the other side is made unimaginably larger, and the answer doesn't move.
The sutra doesn't add a new argument; it turns the volume up on the same one until the size of the pile stops mattering.
The treasure side keeps growing, and it's still the wrong kind of thing. Grains can be counted, at least in principle. Gifts can be counted.
What a few lines of understanding do in a person, passed on at the right moment, isn't on that scale at all.

how: Images like the sands of the Ganges appear across Mahayana sutras, and teachers use them to point past ordinary measuring; in this section the image serves to honor keeping and sharing the teaching.

games.q: what does “sands of the ganges” mean?
o: the sacred sand pilgrims carry home from the river
a sand offering poured at temples on holy days
a number too vast to count, like sand in countless rivers

p: as many as the grains in it
a good man or a good woman

s: the sutra names both a good man and a good woman
here and elsewhere in the sutra, both are named.
section eleven changes the answer from section eight
the treasure side grows unimaginably larger, and four lines still outweigh it.
Subhuti says the sand in all those rivers would be little
very much, he says. the rivers alone would be beyond counting.

games.q: the treasure side of the scale grows from one world system to worlds as many as the sand in countless Ganges rivers. what happens on the other side?
o: the four lines are finally outweighed.
four lines, kept and explained, still weigh more.
the sutra says the two are equal.
games.why: the answer doesn't move. keeping even four lines and explaining them to others is still the greater merit.

practice: The sutra has spent a whole section on numbers too big to hold, so go the other way: let one good thing in your life come to mind, a person, a meal, a morning, a few words that once helped.
Don't add a second or rank it; just hold the one, and let it be enough, the way four lines were enough. If the list starts to grow, smile at it, and come back to the one.

wordCard.voice: Sands of the Ganges. As many rivers as the Ganges has grains, worlds of treasure for each grain, and still four lines passed on are worth more. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Ganges; the sutra measures the immeasurable by its sand.

carryVoice: Your line: more than the sand. Some things never fit on a scale. Rest well; more tomorrow.
